title: Reasons for deaths await inquest stage
article: An explanation of how two people died in RCMP custody on the same weekend in separate incidents won't be made until a coroner's inquest, police said this morning.

The deaths of Heather Lynn Benson, 37, and Clark Edward Whitehouse, 34, are high on the priority list for the Yukon RCMP's major crimes and traffic analyst units, Sgt. Pat Egan told a press conference this morning.
Once the RCMP concludes their investigations, they will be filing their reports with the coroner's office.
Meanwhile, the Yukon coroner will conduct a parallel investigation, and the file will also be reviewed by a Mountie from an Outside division.
"It is standard practice that it will be reviewed by an officer from another division," Egan told reporters today.

Coroner's inquests are required by law in cases of in-custody deaths. The details of the incidents last weekend will be made public at that time, Egan said, declining to provide any more details about how the two people died.
It's impossible to tell at this point how long it may be until an inquest can be held, said Egan.
In the two most recent RCMP custody deaths, coroner's inquests were held between two and three years later.
Benson was killed along the South Klondike Highway early Saturday morning after the police cruiser she was a passenger in crashed and flipped. She died at the scene.
The driver, Const. Jeff Monkman of the Carcross RCMP, had been transporting Benson to Whitehorse for a bail hearing after the Tagish woman was arrested in a drug investigation earlier that morning.
The next afternoon, as the RCMP traffic reconstructionist headed back to Whitehouse after finishing his examination of the previous day's crash scene, he tried to pull Whitehouse over.
He'd seen the man breaking a traffic law, and put on his lights and siren, but was unable to get the Whitehorse man to stop.
Whitehouse turned his black pickup down Lewes Lake Road and fled on foot. In the foot chase, the officer could see Whitehouse ingesting a substance police later came to believe was cocaine.
The fleeing man was combative, and the officer had to use his Taser, or "stun gun", to subdue and arrest him, Egan said Monday.

It wasn't until a few minutes later when the policeman had walked Whitehouse back to the police cruiser and sat him in the back seat when he noticed the man was in medical distress and foaming at the mouth.
Despite efforts to revive him, he was declared dead at Whitehorse General Hospital after being transported back into town by ambulance.
An autopsy is scheduled on Benson's body for today, said chief coroner Sharon Hanley.
The same procedure for Whitehouse's remains is set for tomorrow.
